title: Athletic pseudonephritis in male cross-country ultra-marathoners: a comparative observational study
claims: Twenty male Taiwanese ultra-marathoners were studied before and immediately after a 100 km cross-country trail race.
No participant had urinary red blood cell counts above the reference interval (≥3 cells per high-power field) before the race; post-race, 12 of 20 finishers (60%) had hematuria.
Post-race urine showed statistically significant increases in red blood cells, myoglobin, protein, microalbumin, specific gravity, osmolality and creatinine compared with pre-race values.
Running speed was not associated with the degree of hematuria (p = 0.368), proteinuria or myoglobinuria.
The authors note that post-exercise hematuria and proteinuria are usually temporary and resolve within a few days without medical support.
The introduction cites that acute kidney injury criteria are met in approximately 16%–50% of athletes participating in long-distance races.
